rule_message.title: Small Grid
rule_message.message: This kernel grid is too small to fill the available resources on this device, resulting in only 0.96 full waves across all SMs. Look at @section:LaunchStats:Launch Statistics@ for more details.

focus_metrics.name: launch__waves_per_multiprocessor
focus_metrics.info: Increase the number of waves per SM towards 1

rule_message.message: Every scheduler is capable of issuing one instruction per cycle, but for this workload each scheduler only issues an instruction every 5.0 cycles. This might leave hardware resources underutilized and may lead to less optimal performance. Out of the maximum of 12 warps per scheduler, this workload allocates an average of 2.56 active warps per scheduler, but only an average of 0.24 warps were eligible per cycle. Eligible warps are the subset of active warps that are ready to issue their next instruction. Every cycle with no eligible warp results in no instruction being issued and the issue slot remains unused. To increase the number of eligible warps, avoid possible load imbalances due to highly different execution durations per warp. Reducing stalls indicated on the @section:WarpStateStats:Warp State Statistics@ and @section:SourceCounters:Source Counters@ sections can help, too.

focus_metrics.name: smsp__issue_active.avg.per_cycle_active
focus_metrics.info: Increase the average number of instructions issued per cycle

rule_message.title: Wait Stalls
rule_message.message: On average, each warp of this workload spends 4.2 cycles being stalled waiting on a fixed latency execution dependency. Typically, this stall reason should be very low and only shows up as a top contributor in already highly optimized kernels. Try to hide the corresponding instruction latencies by increasing the number of active warps, restructuring the code or unrolling loops. Furthermore, consider switching to lower-latency instructions, e.g. by making use of fast math compiler options. For example, FFMA-to-FFMA dependency latency is 4 cycles. This stall type represents about 32.2% of the total average of 12.9 cycles between issuing two instructions.

focus_metrics.name: smsp__issue_active.avg.per_cycle_active
focus_metrics.info: Increase the average number of instructions issued per cycle

focus_metrics.name: smsp_average_wait
focus_metrics.info: Decrease the number of cycles spent in wait stalls

rule_message.message: Check the @section:SourceCounters:Warp Stall Sampling (All Samples)@ table for the top stall locations in your source based on sampling data. The @url:Profiling Guide:https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-reference@ provides more details on each stall reason.

rule_message.title: Balanced
rule_message.message: Tensor is the highest-utilized pipeline (56.7%) based on elapsed cycles in the workload, taking into account the rates of its different instructions. It is the logical aggregation of individual tensor pipelines. It's dominated by its Tensor (FP) sub-pipeline. It is well-utilized, but should not be a bottleneck. Based on the number of executed instructions, the highest utilized pipeline (56.7%) is Tensor (FP). It executes 16-bit floating point tensor operations. Comparing the two, the overall pipeline utilization appears to be caused by frequent, low-latency instructions. See the @url:Profiling Guide:https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-decoder@ or hover over the pipeline name to understand the workloads handled by each pipeline. The @section:InstructionStats:Instruction Statistics@ section shows the mix of executed instructions for this workload. Check the @section:WarpStateStats:Warp State Statistics@ section for which reasons cause warps to stall.

focus_metrics.info: Try to decrease the utilization of the busiest pipeline (currently: Tensor)

result_tables.title: Most frequently executed instructions for pipeline Tensor

rule_message.title: L2 Global Load Access Pattern
rule_message.message: The memory access pattern for global loads from L2 might not be optimal. On average, only 31.9 of the 32 bytes transmitted per sector are utilized by each thread. This applies to the 55.8% of sectors missed in L1TEX. This could possibly be caused by a stride between threads. Check the @section:SourceCounters:Source Counters@ section for uncoalesced global loads.
